Narada, filled with joy, controls his speech and bows to the manifested supreme deity.

The deity explains his nature as imperceptible by senses, beyond the three gunas (qualities), pervading all, the witness, and the world soul, indestructible when bodies perish, unborn, enduring, eternal, beyond qualities, and indivisible.

extraction_text: The narrator explains that on the lovely Meru mountain frequented by Siddhas and Caranas, he taught the four Vedas and the Mahabharata as the fifth Veda.
The narrator states that while studying the Vedas, the same doubt raised today appeared, and they asked their teacher who answered it.
The narrator promises to relate what he heard to the descendant of Bharata.
Vyasa, the auspicious son of Parashara, dispeller of all ignorance and darkness, answers his students' questions.
Vyasa explains that through severe ascetic practice, he gained knowledge of past, present, and future.
Vyasa practiced asceticism, controlled his senses, and obtained the favor of Narayana on the shores of the Milk Ocean.
Knowledge of past, present, and future manifested according to Vyasa's wish, and he offers to narrate what he saw with the eye of knowledge about the beginning of the kalpa to remove their doubts.
Vyasa begins his cosmic narration about the Supreme Soul, called the Great Person, from whom the unmanifest (primordial matter) arose.
From the unmanifest, the manifest arose for world creation, with Aniruddha (the Great Soul) manifesting and creating the progenitor Brahma.
From ego (self-awareness) arose the five great elements: earth, wind, space, water, and fire.
After creating the five elements, their qualities were created, and from them arose eight forms: Marici, Angiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Vasistha, and the self-born Manu of great soul.
World progenitor Brahma created the Vedas, Vedic branches, sacrifices, and sacrificial branches for world prosperity, with everything in the world arising from the eight progenitors.
Rudra, characterized by anger, arose and created ten other Rudras, making eleven Rudras total who are known as shape-changers.
All the Rudras, progenitors, and deities approached Brahma for world prosperity, asking how to exercise their authority and protect it.
Brahma agrees with the deities and suggests seeking shelter with the unmanifest Great Person, witness of the world, to learn what is beneficial.
Sages and deities go with Brahma to the northern shore of the Milk Ocean for the world's benefit.
They practice the severe asceticism called Great Vow as prescribed by Brahma, with upward gaze, raised arms, standing on one foot, concentrated and meditative like stakes.
The gods and sages performed severe austerities for one thousand divine years.
A sweet voice, consistent with the Vedas and Vedangas, spoke to them.
The divine voice welcomed them and praised their austerities performed for the world's benefit.
The divine voice instructed them to worship and make offerings in sacrifices.
The gods, sages, and Brahma were filled with joy and performed Vishnu's sacrifice according to Vedic rules.
The formless, gracious Supreme Lord appeared in the sky and spoke to the gods.
The Supreme Lord expressed pleasure with their offerings and explained the fruits of their actions.
The Supreme Lord declared that through his grace, the gods would receive offerings in all ages and maintain the world.
The Supreme Lord created the Vedas, sacrifices, and herbs for people to use correctly to please the gods.
The Supreme Lord created the gods with worldly nature to work for the world's benefit until the end of the age.
Seven sages (Marichi, Angiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasishtha) were created from the mind.
Seven other sages (Sana, Sanatsujata, Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumara, Kapila, and Sanatana) were created as Brahma's mind-born sons.
The teachers gained knowledge from childhood and followed the path of renunciation (出世法).

The three qualities (三性) originate from the unmanifest (未显者), and the knower of the field (知领域者, soul) is above the unmanifest. The speaker identifies as the knower of the field, making it difficult to return to the path of action.

attributes.concept: Philosophical explanation of qualities and soul

extraction_text: The speaker declares that Brahma (梵天) is the world's teacher and creator, the parent and ancestor of all, and will grant favors to all beings as commanded.
Rudra (楼陀罗) is born from Brahma's forehead, obedient to Brahma's commands, and will grant favors to all beings.
The speaker commands the gods to go forth and perform their duties, determining the actions, goals, and lifespans of all beings.

The speaker describes the four ages: Satya Yuga (圆满时代) with complete dharma and no animal sacrifice, Treta Yuga (三分时代) with three Vedas and animal sacrifice, Dvapara Yuga (二分时代) with half dharma, and Kali Yuga (迦利时代) with one-fourth dharma.
The gods ask what they should do when dharma is reduced to one-fourth.
The speaker (吉祥薄伽梵) instructs the gods to go where the Vedas, sacrifice, austerity, truth, self-control, and non-violence are practiced, avoiding unrighteous behavior.
The gods and sages accept the teachings, pay homage, and depart to their desired places.
After the gods leave, Brahma remains alone, wishing to see the Lord in the form of Aniruddha.
The Lord reveals a giant horse-headed form (Hayagriva) holding a water pot and rosary, reciting the Vedas.
Brahma, seeing the infinite Hayagriva, bows with folded hands for the world's welfare. The Lord embraces him and speaks.
The Lord instructs Brahma to establish all worldly actions and ways, becoming the sustainer and teacher of all beings, and promises to appear if divine work is hindered.
The horse-headed Lord disappears, and Brahma returns to his world after receiving the teachings.
The Lord (Narayana, with lotus navel) is described as eternally accepting offerings in sacrifices, the refuge for those seeking immortality, and the origin, middle, and end of all beings.
At the end of an age, he sleeps and withdraws all worlds; at the beginning of an age, he awakens and creates all worlds.
He is praised as the god free from qualities, full of virtues, unborn, with cosmic form, and the home of all celestial beings.
He is described as the lord of the five elements, the Rudras, the Adityas, the Vasus, the Ashvins, the Maruts, the Vedas, sacrifices, and Vedangas.

attributes.action: Description of lordship over various divine beings and knowledge systems

extraction_text: He is described as Hari, residing in the ocean, with matted hair like munja grass, peaceful-minded, teaching all beings the path to liberation.

attributes.action: Description of form and teaching role

extraction_text: He is described as the lord of austerities, power, fame, speech, and rivers; with conch-shaped hair, incarnated as a boar and a fish, wise; the sun, horse-headed, maintaining four forms.
He is described as the mystery, seen only through knowledge; both imperishable and perishable; the eternal god pervading everything.
The speaker states he previously saw all this with the eye of knowledge and now tells it truthfully when asked.
The speaker instructs students to serve the great lord Hari, recite the Vedas, and worship him according to rules.
Suta reports that the wise Veda compiler Vyasa told all this to his students and his son Shuka who knows the highest law.
Suta states that their teacher and students together praised this god with Rigvedic verses.
Suta tells King Janamejaya that the island-born teacher Vyasa previously told him all this, and now he tells it to the king who asked.

Benefits are described for those who hear, recite, and worship Hari: safety, vigor, strength, beauty, healing, liberation, wish-fulfillment, longevity, knowledge for Brahmins, victory for Kshatriyas, wealth for Vaishyas, happiness for Shudras, children for the childless, good husbands for maidens, safe childbirth, fertility for barren women, safe travel, and happiness for devotees.
Conclusion identifies this as Chapter 327 of the Shanti Parva in the Mahabharata.
